taxonomic_note: Modern accepted placement is Bouteloua dactyloides; many Texas sources still use the long-familiar synonym Buchloe dactyloides.
look_here_first: START AT GROUND LEVEL: Buffalograss is a short stoloniferous sod-forming grass. When flowering, look for raised pale comb-like MALE heads (two well photographed by Jim Conrad in Uvalde County), then search deeper among the short leaves for VERY DIFFERENT compact FEMALE bur-like clusters (shown in a licensed source comparison: LEFT normal female, RIGHT normal male, MIDDLE fungus-infected abnormal plant). Usually sexes occur on separate plants, but mixed-sex exceptions exist. Unlike blue grama's prominent curved eyebrows, the soil-level runners/sex-specific heads are stronger buffalograss clues. An attached rooting stolon with node remains unphotographed.
project_tracker_diagnostic: perennial mat-forming shortgrass with stolons rooting at nodes; usually dioecious with strongly different male and female inflorescences; female inflorescences compact/bur-like and often partly concealed among leaves; male inflorescences with two or three short flag-like spikes; short ciliate-membranous ligule; low dense turf/sod habit rather than a typical tall bunchgrass

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT Austin Plant Resources Center Flora of Purola Preserve, N. Hays County explicitly records Buchloe dactyloides (accepted Bouteloua dactyloides). Travis — Fowler (2002) documents Buchloe dactyloides as abundant in flat plots at Shield Ranch in western Travis County. Williamson — UT Austin Plant Resources Center Vascular Plants of Williamson County includes the taxon under Buchloe dactyloides; BONAP county mapping independently supports the Texas county distribution.

usually dioecious with strongly different male and female inflorescences

crew_field_steps: Check the soil-level habit: buffalograss often makes short connected sod rather than an upright tuft.
Find an aboveground horizontal stolon and photograph it rooted at a node; current habit photo does not isolate a root.
Identify flower SEX before interpreting heads. Male: small terminal units; Female: compact burs low in foliage. Photograph both separately.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Low connected turf with actual creeping stolon traced from crown to node.
True horizontal rooting stolon node at scale.
MALE raised seedhead with short flowering units (label male only after verifying actual flowers).
FEMALE compact low burr-like seedheads with scale.
Sideoats/blue grama matched head shapes to teach crew contrast.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Blue grama has a prominent curved terminal rooster-comb inflorescence and generally forms a tuft or short rhizomatous crown, while buffalograss spreads by stolons and has distinct male and female heads. Curlymesquite also mats but often has visibly hairy stolon nodes and a different flower head. Bermudagrass often has several finger-like racemes and an introduced lawn-grass context; stolons alone are not proof of buffalograss.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Grama field check — Buffalograss
steps: FIRST at soil: find a LOW connected mat. Photograph ACTUAL creeping aboveground stolon with the true node and any attached adventitious roots; existing mat image does not demonstrate roots.
SECOND on reproductive plant: distinguish upright MALE flag-like 1–5 comb branches and orange/yellow pollen-bearing anthers from short, partly concealed FEMALE bur-like green heads near leaves.
For the photographed TEXAS male plant, the Jim Conrad image links the whole flowering culm to close male combs; identify anthers only in the close image, not a distant seed head.

THIRD compare the new 3-panel SEX IMAGE: LEFT = uninfected FEMALE; CENTER = fungus-infected/sex-altered male, ABNORMAL; RIGHT = uninfected MALE with orange anthers. Never teach center as a normal female.
FOURTH inspect grass leaf collar; Jim Conrad photo shows actual stiff short fringe and longer side hairs. Collar hairs support grass ID but do not alone certify buffalograss.
FIFTH separate blue grama (prominent long curved eyebrows and less of a creeping stoloniferous mat) and curlymesquite (other native stoloniferous mat with different flowering head).
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Blue grama has a prominent curved terminal rooster-comb inflorescence and generally forms a tuft or short rhizomatous crown, while buffalograss spreads by stolons and has distinct male and female heads. Curlymesquite also mats but often has visibly hairy stolon nodes and a different flower head. Bermudagrass often has several finger-like racemes and an introduced lawn-grass context; stolons alone are not proof of buffalograss.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: BUFFALOGRASS vs OTHER GRAMAS — ground-hugging branching STOLONS and distinct flower SEX help; buffalograss is USUALLY DIOECIOUS, not obligately always: male raised combs typically 1–5 branches bearing pollen/anthers, female low compact bur-like clusters usually hidden in upper foliage. Both sexes can occur on one plant occasionally (monoecious) and rare perfect flowers are reported. NO FEMALE BUR should be assumed from a male head. Confirm sex on actual flowers, not the plant's location or grass mat shape.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — MAT + FLOWER SEX
field_id_short_tiles.short: Trace an actual creeping stolon, then distinguish raised male combs from concealed female burs.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Buffalograss is a low warm-season perennial spreading into sod by aboveground stolons. Confirm the horizontal runner and rooting node on the SAME plant; the existing mat photo does not expose roots. Flowering plants are usually dioecious: male branches stand above leaves, while female bur-like clusters stay low. Rare mixed-sex plants occur. Species panels 1–2 show a Texas male plant and male heads; panel 3 is a comparison image, not a local female voucher.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD-READY GROWTH/SEX CUES; ROOTED RUNNER + LOCAL FEMALE MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Short hair-fringed or ciliate-membranous ligule, generally less than ~1 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: At the inside blade–sheath junction separate the actual ligule from long side hairs. South Dakota State describes a hair fringe <1 mm, while a regional Colorado treatment describes a ~0.5–1 mm ciliate membrane; record this source wording rather than asserting an exact membrane edge from the photograph. Species panel 4 is a real Jim Conrad Texas collar view, but no millimeter ruler establishes ligule length. Photograph the free inner margin at 10–20×.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL COLLAR PHOTO; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — MEASURED INNER LIGULE

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MALE — COUNT SHORT COMBS AND SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Raised male heads: often 1–3(4) short one-sided branches, each carrying 2-flowered spikelets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: On an attached flowering culm, count the comb-like unilateral branches rather than assuming every comb is a spikelet. Flora of North America describes 1–3(4) branches; South Dakota State gives 2–5 branches about 7–13 mm long. Kew reports male spikelets ~4–5.5 mm, with two florets and two glumes. Existing Texas panels 1–2 visibly show male heads and anthers, not calibrated glumes or floret dissections.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL MALE COMBS PRESENT; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — SCALED ATTACHED SPIKELET

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · MALE — SEPARATE GLUMES AND LEMMAS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Male glumes unequal, roughly ~1.4–5 mm across sources; lemmas 3-veined, without long awns.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Dissect a mature MALE 2-flowered spikelet under a 1-mm scale. South Dakota State reports unequal male glumes about 1.4–3 mm and <5 mm; Kew reports ~4–5.5 mm whole male spikelets and 3-veined awnless male lemmas. Do not transfer FEMALE hardened-glume teeth to a male lemma, or draw vein arrows on intact comb photos. Record male anther color only where visible.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED MALE ANATOMY; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — DISSECTED GLUMES/LEMMAS

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · FEMALE — OPEN A HEALTHY BUR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Low female clusters contain one-flowered spikelets; hardened upper glumes form three-toothed burs.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Seek intact, healthy female heads hidden in foliage, not the conspicuous male combs. Kew describes female spikelets ~3–4 mm, a hardened ~3–4 mm upper glume with a three-part apex, and a 3-veined fertile lemma ~2.5–3.5 mm; the lower glume is much reduced or obscure. Flora of North America describes bur-like branches ~2.5–4.5 mm with often 3–5 spikelets. The comparison triptych's CENTER is fungus-altered and must NEVER be presented as normal female anatomy. Female glume teeth are not equivalent to a long awn on a male lemma.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE-BASED FEMALE ANATOMY; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — HEALTHY TEXAS FEMALE + DISSECTION

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES + PUBLIC GATE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Blue grama's curved terminal eyebrows and bermudagrass's fingers differ from buffalograss's sex-specific heads.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Blue grama (Bouteloua gracilis) generally carries 1–3 prominent curved eyebrow-like branches rather than separate male comb and concealed female bur morphologies. Curlymesquite (Hilaria belangeri) also forms stoloniferous mats but has a different reproductive head. Introduced bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) has radiating slender terminal racemes and a hair-fringed collar. Require a linked rooted runner, opened ligule and sex-verified reproductive organs; all six archived source-specific photo licenses and the seven-panel gallery still require public-rights and responsive arrow QA. Keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
